Article Title: 'Jewel of India': PM Modi, Rahul Gandhi, Rajnath Singh pay tributes to Nehru on birth anniversary
Article Text:
Rahul remembers Nehru as 'jewel of India' (Picture from X handle of Supriya Shrinate)

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday paid tribute to former Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru on his 137th birth anniversary, which is also observed as Children's Day across the country.In a post on X, PM Modi said, "Paying tribute to former PM Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru on his birth anniversary."Defence minister Rajnath Singh also paid homage to the country's first prime minister, recalling his contribution to India's freedom struggle and his leadership during the early years of independent India.In a post on X, Rajnath said, "On the birth anniversary of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru Ji, I pay my tributes to him. His contribution to India’s freedom struggle and his leadership as the first Prime Minister of independent India left an enduring imprint on the formative years of our nation."Lok Sabha leader of opposition and former Congress chief Rahul Gandhi also paid tribute to Jawaharlal Nehru on his birth anniversary.In a post on X, Rahul described Nehru as the "jewel of India" and the country's first prime minister.He said freedom was not the destination but "a milestone in the nation's new journey", adding that Swaraj was not merely about power but about every citizen's participation and responsibility towards the country's future.Rahul also recalled Nehru's vision of India as an idea built on diversity, democracy and equality."Their dream of a modern, scientific, progressive, and self-confident India remains our inspiration today," he said, adding that efforts to build such an India would be the "true tribute" to Nehru.November 14 is celebrated as Children's Day in India to mark the birth anniversary of Nehru, who was popularly known as 'Chacha Nehru' because of his affection for children.After Nehru's death, it was unanimously decided to observe his birthday as ' Bal Diwas ' or Children's Day in India. He was born on November 14, 1889, in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh, and died on May 27, 1964.Nehru became India's first prime minister on August 15, 1947, after playing an active role in the country's freedom struggle.Schools across the country organise various activities for students on the occasion, including games and competitions. Government bodies also pay tribute to the former prime minister and hold commemorative events.The United Nations declared November 20 as Universal Children's Day in 1954. India initially observed Children's Day on the same date.However, following Nehru's death in 1964, Parliament unanimously passed a resolution to mark his birth anniversary on November 14 as National Children's Day.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday paid tribute to former Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru on his 137th birth anniversary. Defence minister Rajnath Singh also paid homage to the country's first prime minister. November 14 is celebrated as Children's Day in India to mark the birth anniversary of Nehru.

Article Title: 'Visa matters are sovereign': MEA responds after 115 foreign speakers denied nod for Congress event
Article Text:
Political backlash

NEW DELHI: The Ministry of external affairs (MEA) on Friday defended India's visa decisions, saying these are "sovereign functions" of every government. The response came amid allegations that more than 100 foreign speakers invited to the Congress-organised Bharat Summit in Hyderabad were denied entry into India or had their visas cancelled."I would like to say, and all of you are aware, that visa matters are sovereign functions of any country or any government. So that is what I have to say," MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said during his the bi-weekly media briefing.The MEA's response came amid allegations by Congress leaders that several foreign delegates who had received prior clearance from the ministry were subsequently denied entry into India or had their visas revoked. The opposition has alleged that the decisions were taken following instructions from the Union ministry of home affairs (MHA).The two-day Bharat Summit 2026 is being held in Hyderabad on November 13 and 14, bringing together around 1,000 delegates, policymakers and thinkers from 70 countries. Organised by the Congress and the Telangana government, the summit features discussions on global geopolitics, democracy, climate change, artificial intelligence and progressive politics.The controversy has particularly brought Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng into focus, after she claimed that her Indian visa was cancelled shortly before her scheduled departure for Hyderabad, where she was due to participate in a panel discussion on media and press freedom at the Bharat Summit.In a post on X, Lyng said she had received a visa from the Indian embassy in Norway and was scheduled to travel to Hyderabad on Friday. However, she alleged that her visa was cancelled shortly before she was due to leave for the airport, citing "orders from above" in the ministry of home affairs.Lyng's case has also drawn attention because of her earlier interaction with Prime Minister Narendra Modi during his visit to Oslo in May. The Norwegian journalist had questioned PM Modi on press freedom and his reluctance to take questions from journalists during the visit.The reported visa cancellations have triggered a political row, with opposition leaders questioning the government's decision and alleging that foreign journalists and speakers were being prevented from attending the international gathering.Telangana CM A Revanth Reddy launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi, accusing him of having a dictatorial mindset over the alleged restrictions on foreign journalists attending the Bharat Summit.In a post on X, Reddy alleged that some journalists were stopped from entering India by the ministry of home Affairs despite having received visas. Questioning the reported action, he said, "Is asking Modi ji a question a crime? It is journalists' responsibility to ask questions. Whether to answer them is up to Modi ji."Defending the summit, Reddy said the Invest Telangana Global Summit 2026 aimed to attract investments and generate employment for skilled and unskilled youth, while showcasing Hyderabad's cultural and technological development to representatives from 70 countries.Congress MP Shashi Tharoor also criticised the reported visa cancellations, describing them as a "disappointing footnote" to the Bharat Summit."It is completely unclear under what provision of law the government has taken such a drastic step," he said, adding that reversing the decision was impossible as the conference was scheduled to conclude the following day.Tharoor further criticised the development, saying, "What a shame that a proud democracy has become so insecure that it must stifle any voices it fears will be critical!"Meanwhile, former foreign secretary Kanwal Sibal took a contrasting position, criticising the Norwegian side over the controversy and calling its conduct "unacceptable".In a post on X, Sibal said, "The Norwegians are being very presumptuous. Trying to put us on the mat."Suggesting a tougher response, he added, "Our answer to this should be to tighten up grant of visas to Norwegian journalists."The BJP, meanwhile, defended the visa cancellations, branding the gathering an "Anti-Bharat Summit" and accusing the Congress of bringing together radical Left and anti-India groups.
Article Summary: The Ministry of external affairs (MEA) on Friday defended India's visa decisions. The response came amid allegations that more than 100 foreign speakers invited to the Congress-organised Bharat Summit in Hyderabad were denied entry into India or had their visas cancelled. The opposition has alleged that the decisions were taken following instructions from the Union ministry of home affairs.

Article Title: Women at the controls, solar power on the rooftops: What makes Pune Metro's Pink Line special
Article Text:
PM Modi virtually inaugurated Pune Metro's Pink Line on November 3 and commercial operations began the following day

Why Pune needed the Metro

Why the Pink Line matters

Pune Metro's Pink Line is the network's third corridor to open and the first to pass through Hinajwadi, the city's IT hub

Pune Metro's Pink Line: A timeline of the project

Women at the controls

What makes Pune Metro's Pink Line special

A Metro corridor powered partly by solar energy

Pune Metro's Pink Line in numbers

India's first Metro project under the 2017 Metro policy's PPP framework

Beyond Metro connectivity

The way forward for Pune Metro's Pink Line

On November 3, Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated and laid the foundation stones for Pune Metro projects worth around Rs 21,800 crore.The project he inaugurated was Line 3 of Pune Metro, popularly known as the Pink Line. Built at a cost of approximately Rs 8,300 crore, the 23.2-km corridor connects Maan, on Pune's northwestern outskirts, with the District Court Metro station in Shivajinagar, central Pune. Also known as Civil Court station, it serves as an interchange with Line 1 (Purple Line) and Line 2 (Aqua Line), connecting passengers to other parts of the Metro network.PM Modi described the Pink Line as "so special". Beyond the connectivity it offers, the corridor stands out for its distinctive approach to operations, infrastructure development and sustainability.Over the years, Pune's population has grown significantly, with people from other parts of Maharashtra as well as outside the state migrating to the city. Pune was home to over 12 lakh people in 1981, according to that year's national census. The figure rose to more than 31 lakh in 2011, the latest national census, meaning the city added around 19 lakh people in 30 years – an increase of nearly 160%.Migration to Pune and the subsequent population expansion have largely been driven by the growth of its IT, manufacturing and educational sectors.Pune is counted among India's leading IT hubs, alongside Bengaluru and Hyderabad. Several prominent colleges and universities are also located in the city, further contributing to its growing population and demand for public transport.Against this backdrop, the foundation stone for the first phase of Pune Metro, comprising the Purple and Aqua lines, was laid in December 2016. The network's commercial operations commenced in March 2022.Although the launch of Pune Metro improved connectivity, several important areas remained outside its network, limiting its reach. The Pink Line addresses part of this gap by connecting Hinjawadi to the existing Metro network.The significance of the Pink Line extends beyond it being just another corridor of the Pune Metro network. Before the route opened to the public on November 4, a day after its inauguration, the network had no connectivity to Hinjawadi, one of Pune's largest employment centres and a major IT hub. The area houses offices of major technology companies such as Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and Cognizant.The Purple Line, which runs between Pimpri-Chinchwad and Swargate, and the Aqua Line, connecting Vanaz and Ramwadi, were the only two operational corridors at the time. As a result, software professionals living in other parts of Pune had to rely on road transport to commute to Hinjawadi or relocate closer to their workplaces.With 17 of the corridor's stations now operational and the remaining six scheduled to open in March 2027, commuters can interchange at District Court station in Shivajinagar and travel directly to Hinjawadi, making daily commutes more seamless.Commuters have also expressed hope that the Pink Line will ease congestion on roads leading to Hinjawadi.“The entire stretch from Wakad to Hinjawadi Phase-II remains busy and chaotic during rush hours. We expect relief from these snarls,” a commuter told The Times of India in an earlier report.Another commuter, who travels by bike to his workplace at Balewadi near Hinjawadi, noted that the Metro journey took nearly as much time as his two-wheeler commute but offered greater comfort.“My travel time by bike would be around 30-45 minutes, depending on the traffic. It took about 30 minutes to reach Balewadi by Metro. There was no huge drop in the travel time, but the overall comfort in Metro was much more,” he added.Another important feature of the Pink Line, officials say, is its provision for last-mile connectivity through bus services, dedicated pickup zones for taxis and auto-rickshaws, and cycle parking at stations.With the Pink Line now open, the Aqua and Purple lines being expanded, and a fourth corridor taking shape, the focus will increasingly be on integrating the expanding Metro network with other transport modes to improve connectivity across Pune.In October 2011, a woman loco pilot, Priyanka N, drove the inaugural train of Namma Metro in Bengaluru. Since then, several Metro networks across the country have employed women as train operators.However, Pune has taken this a step further by introducing an entire Metro corridor where all train drivers are women.While other Metro networks in India, including Delhi and Bengaluru, also have corridors designated as the Pink Line, Pune's newest Metro corridor has a special significance attached to the name. Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis said the corridor would be called the Pink Line because its trains would be operated exclusively by women.Nearly 15 years after Priyanka N drove the first Namma Metro train, Pune Metro's Pink Line has become India's first Metro corridor to have an all-women team of train drivers.As many as 90 women have completed training and obtained competency certificates to operate trains on the Hinjawadi–Shivajinagar route. Recruited through campus drives, they underwent classroom instruction, practical sessions and extensive on-track training before being cleared to operate passenger services. The women have since taken charge of regular train operations on the corridor.Overall, the plan is to have 100 women operators on the line, including the 90 already operating trains on it.Having an entire Metro corridor with women at the controls also marks a significant step towards greater representation of women in operational roles in urban rail transport.Another important feature of Pune Metro's Pink Line is that 30% of its energy requirements are expected to be met through solar power. The project also uses a 750V DC third-rail electrification system, which eliminates the need for overhead wires.Tata Power Renewables has received a contract from Pune IT City Metro Rail Ltd, which operates Pune Metro Line 3, to install a 7.67 MWp rooftop solar project. The installation will cover all 23 stations and the Metro depot. The electricity generated will be used for captive consumption. The project is expected to help reduce the corridor's operating costs and dependence on conventional sources of electricity.With this, Pune Metro joins several transport projects in India, including other Metro systems, that use solar power. For instance, as of 2023, 35% of Delhi Metro's total energy consumption came from renewable sources. This included 30% from its off-site solar power plant in Rewa, Madhya Pradesh, 4% from rooftop solar panels and 1% from the waste-to-energy plant in Ghazipur, Delhi.Outside the Metro network, Cochin International Airport in Kerala became the world's first airport to run entirely on solar power with the commissioning of a 12 MWp solar PV power plant in 2015.The solar power component, therefore, adds another dimension to the Pink Line's approach to energy use and operational efficiency.The Pink Line is also significant for the model through which it has been developed. It is India's first Metro rail project to be implemented under the public-private partnership (PPP) framework of the Centre's New Metro Rail Policy, 2017, which aims to encourage private investment in transport infrastructure.While cities such as Mumbai and Hyderabad have previously developed Metro projects under PPP models, Pune's Pink Line is the first to be implemented under the framework of the 2017 policy.The project was developed by Pune IT City Metro Rail Limited, a special-purpose company established as a joint venture between TRIL Urban Transport Private Limited, part of the Tata Group, and Germany's Siemens, in collaboration with the Pune Metropolitan Region Development Authority.Another technological feature of the Pink Line is its Siemens-supplied Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) signalling system. While the existing Purple and Aqua lines also use CBTC systems, these are supplied by France's Alstom.According to Siemens, its CBTC system allows trains to communicate continuously with trackside equipment, enabling high-frequency services while maintaining safe distances between trains. It is designed for semi-automated operations, with provision for a future upgrade to fully automated, driverless operations.The technology adds to the corridor's operational capabilities while leaving scope for greater automation in the future.Despite these features and the integration of Hinjawadi into the Metro network, several challenges remain in improving the overall commuting experience in the city, experts say.For instance, despite the Pink Line reportedly recording a ridership of around 50,000 on its very first day, some passengers raised concerns about gaps in first- and last-mile connectivity.According to Tanzeel Allapur, programme associate at Parisar, a Pune-based NGO working on sustainable urban transport since 1995, the administration cannot limit its idea of a good commuting experience to building new Metro lines alone and must focus on improving connectivity to and from Metro stations.“Finding a connecting bus or shared auto, figuring out where to board, and navigating the surroundings of a Metro station all add to the mental effort involved in making that journey. The administration needs to focus on reducing both the physical friction and the cognitive load involved in these transfers,” she told The Times of India.Echoing this view, Jagannarayan Padmanabhan, senior director at Crisil Intelligence, stressed the importance of seamless connectivity rather than simply adding more routes.“Seamless connectivity with PMPML buses, feeder services, autos and shared mobility, supported by integrated ticketing and pedestrian infrastructure, is essential,” he added.Although it is still early days for the Pink Line, improved connectivity and integration with other modes of transport could further build on the benefits it brings to Pune's public transport network.Looking ahead, transport activist Ranjit Gadgil, who heads Parisar, said that with the Pink Line now operational alongside the two existing corridors, authorities must introduce measures to curb private vehicle use to reduce congestion, pollution and road accidents.“With the addition of the Pink Line to the existing two corridors, it is high time the city started implementing measures to curb vehicle use. These could include on-street parking charges, low-emission zones and street designs that prioritise the safety and movement of pedestrians, cyclists and buses rather than allocating more space to motor vehicles,” he added.Ultimately, the Pink Line offers Pune an opportunity to make public transport a more convenient choice for commuters. Its connectivity to Hinjawadi, in particular, could encourage more people working in the IT hub to consider the Metro for their daily journeys.But the real measure of the Pink Line's success will be whether it can persuade more people to leave their cars and two-wheelers behind and make public transport their preferred choice.
Article Summary: PM Modi virtually inaugurated Pune Metro's Pink Line on November 3. The 23.2-km corridor connects Maan, on Pune's northwestern outskirts, with the District Court Metro station in Shivajinagar, central Pune. It is the network's third corridor to open and the first to pass through Hinajwadi, the city's IT hub.

Article Title: From Australian chana to Canadian masoor: NITI Aayog flags India's food import dependence
Article Text:
Lahiri said he was surprised to learn that chana (gram) consumed in India comes from Australia,

NEW DELHI: India may not yet be fully secure in meeting its food requirements, with heavy dependence on imports for essential commodities such as edible oils and pulses, NITI Aayog vice-chairman Ashok Kumar Lahiri said on Friday.Speaking at an event in Delhi, Lahiri said India imports more than half of its edible oil requirements and relies on other countries for several pulses.He questioned whether the country was sufficiently prepared to deal with disruptions in global supplies and sudden price increases."We are talking about Viksit Krishi in Viksit Bharat in 2047. As we move towards Viksit Bharat at 2047, are we secure regarding our food supply across the various products? Perhaps not as yet," he said.Lahiri said he was surprised to learn that chana (gram) consumed in India comes from Australia, while masoor dal is imported from Australia and Canada. Some pulses also come from Myanmar, African countries and Russia, according to news agency PTI."Now you can ask what is wrong with India importing edible oils or oil seeds from Indonesia, Malaysia, Argentina, Brazil, Russia, and Ukraine, and pulses from Australia, Canada, Myanmar, Africa, and Russia," Lahiri said."The problem is, first, the issue of vulnerability to global supply disruptions or price shocks," he added.India meets more than half of its edible oil demand through imports. These imports are estimated at 17 million metric tonnes, worth around $20 billion, Lahiri said.India is also the world's largest producer and consumer of pulses, accounting for nearly a fourth of global consumption. The country consumes around 25-27 million tonnes of pulses every year."For our dal-chawal or dal-roti, we require pulses and edible oils. Any disruption of supply of these essential commodities or price shock can assume the gravity of a strategic disaster," he said.Lahiri said reducing dependence on imports would require greater focus on domestic production of pulses and edible oils. He pointed to the need to diversify crops and reduce the dominance of wheat and paddy in Indian agriculture.Since pulses and oilseed crops generally require less water, he said, promoting their cultivation could also help address agricultural challenges.The NITI Aayog vice-chairman also stressed the need to reduce and eliminate waste in Indian agriculture.
Article Summary: India imports more than half of its edible oil requirements and relies on other countries for several pulses. Lahiri said he was surprised to learn that chana (gram) consumed in India comes from Australia. He questioned whether the country was sufficiently prepared to deal with disruptions in global supplies and sudden price increases.

Article Title: Breakthrough HIV drug sees 18 patent filings, may delay affordable generics
Article Text:
An unusually high 18 patent applications filed in India for lenacapavir

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: An unusually high 18 patent applications filed in India for lenacapavir, a breakthrough HIV therapy, have raised concerns that these could prolong market exclusivity, delay affordable generics, keep prices high and restrict patient access. Contesting the move, patient groups and civil society have filed opposition with the regulatory authorities, arguing the applications lack novelty and inventive steps.Lenacapavir, a long-acting injectable, administered twice yearly for both HIV prevention and treatment, a medicine designated as essential by WHO.Last year, US FDA approved Gilead Sciences' lenacapavir as the first and only twice-yearly injectable pre-exposure prophylaxis to reduce sexually acquired HIV. Gilead has filed at least 18 patent pleas till date in India, covering different aspects of it, including the base compound, salt forms, formulations, dosing regimens, compositions, and methods of use."The pattern of filings reflects a systematic strategy to create layered patent protection around a single medicine, with the effect of deterring generic entry and prolonged monopoly control beyond the standard 20-year patent term.Such practices, also referred to as "evergreening", whereby multiple secondary patents covering minor variations in forms, formulations, or used or pursued to extend exclusivity," KM Gopakumar, senior researcher and legal advisor at TWN told TOI.In a letter to the department for promotion of industry and internal trade, patient groups demanded that the patent office must rigorously examine and reject the company's secondary patent applications.Dr Reddy's is one of six generic manufacturers which has signed voluntary licenses with Gilead to manufacture and commercialise lenacapavir across 120 low and lower middle income countries, including India. The generic injection is projected to cost approximately $40 per person annually. So, apart from the voluntary licence holders, no other generics can manufacture and market the drug.Further, the patents, if granted, are set to expire in 2042, 28 years after the first application was filed. "Granting these patents would legitimise Gilead's evergreening strategy," Prathibha Sivasubramanian of Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, told TOI.
Article Summary: An unusually high 18 patent applications filed in India for lenacapavir, a breakthrough HIV therapy. Concerns that these could prolong market exclusivity, delay affordable generics, keep prices high and restrict patient access. Gilead has filed at least 18 patent pleas till date in India, covering different aspects of it.

Article Title: After EASA concern, Air India asks crew to remain on board till replacement arrives during Europe fuelling halts
Article Text:
How Air India tackled the issues:

NEW DELHI: Air India has asked its cockpit and cabin crew operating flights between India and North America that take a fuelling halt in Europe since the US-Iran war broke out this Feb, to remain on board till the relief crew takes over from them to operate the remaining lag of the flight. The reason: Refuelling takes place during these halts which requires the cockpit to be manned by pilots and/or engineers for the process and since passengers remain on board during this time, cabin crew has to be there to announce precautions like keeping seat belts off.There were some instances when the incoming crew left the aircraft immediately on arrival in Europe. This gap in standard operating procedure (SOP) was detected primarily at Vienna during “EU ramp inspection programme” carried out to do “safety assessment of foreign aircraft” (SAFA). Along with cabin condition issues, this led to European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) SAFA score of Air India rising to 2.7, indicating safety-related deficiencies.The same was conveyed to the Indian Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), which then swung into action along with AI to rectify the situation. The airline started deploying new or retrofitted aircraft on these routes which largely took care of cabin issues.For fuelling, AI asked its crew to remain on board till the replacement crew arrives.After taking these two steps, AI’s SAFA score has now gone to about 1.4, indicating that the issues that led to the earlier higher score have been largely addressed. “The DGCA did extensive monitoring and ensured AI followed the protocol to a T. Now AI is in the ‘good zone’ of Europe’s SAFA with the score falling from 2.7 earlier to about 1.4,” said people in the know. “Now crew often remains on board for about 1-1.5 hours after landing to oversee the fuelling process till relief crew arrives,” they add.AI’s improved SAFA score comes as a breather for the short-staffed DGCA that has been headed by non-aviation generalists for about two decades now, just ahead of facing an audit by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) from next week. It is also a relief for Air India as it is the only Indian carrier that flies to the US and will be examined closely by FAA for that reason. In operational terms, this should lead to less checks during fuelling stops in Europe and fewer delays on that count during halts there for AI.Refuelling: The SOP is that an engineering team and/or pilots should be in the flight deck when an aircraft is getting refuelled to coordinate with the fuelling staff. The cabin crew has to announce that passengers must not have their seat belts on when fuelling is taking place.The AI circular for pilots, reiterating the incoming set remains on board till it’s replaced by the relief crew. “Before commencing fuelling, the flight deck crew will be informed by engineering. If flight crew are unable to attend the flight deck during refueling, they shall request a qualified engineer to attend the flight deck,” says his circular.It adds: “NO PED (personal electronic devices) NO SMOKING / NO DEVICES / EXIT signs shall be illuminated as an indication to the cabin crew that fuelling is in progress. 'Seat belt' sign must be off. Known high energy equipment such as HF radios shall not be operated (during refuelling).”
Article Summary: Air India has asked its cockpit and cabin crew operating flights between India and North America to remain on board till the relief crew takes over from them. Refuelling takes place during these halts which requires the cockpit to be manned by pilots and/or engineers. The cabin crew has to announce that passengers must not have their seat belts on during fuelling.

Article Title: Row erupts over foreign medicos' 'MD Physician' title
Article Text:
Row erupts over foreign medicos' 'MD Physician' title

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: An 'MD' title after a doctor's name usually signals a postgraduate medical qualification in India. But for some foreign medical graduates, MD (Physician) is the title of their primary medical degree.This difference has triggered a dispute over professional titles, with doctors warning that patients could be misled and foreign medical graduates arguing their qualifications are officially recognised.Dr Dhruv Chauhan, national spokesperson for Junior Doctors' Network (JDN) of Indian Medical Association, flagged the issue in a post on X, alleging some doctors misuse the 'MD' degree title awarded in foreign countries, where it may denote a primary medical qualification equivalent to MBBS in India.He said that using it in professional titles and online biographies could mislead patients and even other doctors, and warned of possible legal consequences. He also advised doctors against such representations.Dr MK Ramesh, president of NMC's Medical Assessment and Rating Board told TOI the issue arises from differences in medical qualification nomenclature across countries. In some countries, the basic medical qualification is called an MD, whereas in India it is MBBS.This distinction needs to be clearly recognised. Some measures have already been taken to address the issue, and further steps will be pursued.A senior doctor said the issue had persisted for nearly a decade despite repeated representations to regulators. "Patients cannot be expected to know the difference," he said.All FMGs Association has defended the use of the title "MD Physician", arguing the qualification is recognised as equivalent to MBBS in India and that graduates should not be branded fraudulent merely for mentioning the degree awarded by their foreign universities.
Article Summary: An 'MD' title after a doctor's name usually signals a postgraduate medical qualification in India. But for some foreign medical graduates, MD (Physician) is the title of their primary medical degree. This difference has triggered a dispute over professional titles, with doctors warning that patients could be misled.

Article Title: AIIMS plans national registry to track poisoning cases
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: AIIMS New Delhi is planning a national system to track poisoning cases across the country, with a proposed National Poisoning Registry that would collect reports of poisoning cases and digitally link poison-control units for real-time reporting.The proposal envisages transforming the National Poisons Information Centre (NPIC) from a 24x7 telephone advisory service into a national nodal network for toxicology, with satellite units connected digitally to the AIIMS centre.Under the proposed system, poisoning cases reported by participating centres could feed into a central database to track emerging trends and improve preparedness. The plan also includes a national antidote bank, analytical testing facility, research and development, real-time reporting software and AI-assisted diagnostic support.Established at AIIMS in 1995, NPIC was India’s first centre of its kind. From a telephone service guiding doctors on emergency poison management, it has grown into a 24x7 toxicology resource receiving calls nationwide. It received over 65,000 calls between 1995 and 2025, involving household products, pesticides, drug overdoses and snake bites.NPIC data show a wide range of exposures, including drugs, agricultural and industrial chemicals, plants, household products and stings and bites.Snake bites were the largest component of sting-and-bite calls in both 2010–19 and 2020–25.The proposed expansion is aimed at moving beyond individual emergency calls to create a broader national picture of poisoning patterns. AIIMS has proposed digitally linking the nodal centre with satellite units, along with analytical testing and a national antidote bank, to strengthen the response to poisoning emergencies.The proposal also seeks wider poison-awareness and capacity-building programmes for children, teachers, parents and occupational workers, along with a National Outreach and Awareness Programme and a dedicated National Poison Awareness Day. As part of the expansion, AIIMS has proposed renaming NPIC as the National Nodal Centre for Toxicological Sciences & Research (NNCTSR).Prof D.S. Arya, Head, Department of Pharmacology and Chief, NPIC, AIIMS, New Delhi, and the team led by Dr Swati Sharma, Senior Scientist and Nodal Officer, NPIC Expansion Programme, Department of Pharmacology, AIIMS, New Delhi.
Article Summary: AIIMS New Delhi is planning a national system to track poisoning cases across the country. A proposed National Poisoning Registry would collect reports of poisoning cases and digitally link poison-control units for real-time reporting. The plan also includes a national antidote bank, analytical testing facility, research and development.

Article Title: Mahadev betting app: CBI raids 33 locations across six states after Chandrakar's extradition

Article Title: Urea overuse in 169 dists raises red flags, CAG probing diversion
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: CAG has initiated an all-India performance audit of fertiliser subsidy, specifically to look into the alleged diversion of subsidised urea in at least 169 districts across a few states, including the possibility of diversion outside the country. The audit, which started in May this year, is likely to be completed by mid-2027 to be tabled by the winter session of Parliament.Govt spends more than Rs 2 lakh crore annually on the subsidised urea, and their overconsumption above the national and state average in some districts has raised concerns within govt. CAG will assess the demand and efficiency of the urea subsidy framework, which is also the terms of reference of the audit.The selected 169 districts to be assessed for alleged diversion, include 149 initially chosen by CAG based on their consumption pattern, which were above the state and national average. Twenty other districts were added later after recommendation from the Centre to examine their consumption pattern. The audit will look into the fertiliser movement mechanism, their transportation arrangements, freight subsidy and associated monitoring and control system.This integrated audit approaches a wider cooperation and participation from different govt departments, like the GST network, agriculture ministry, railways and others, who will assist the auditors in its assessment of the fertiliser control system and the efficacy of the regulators.The finance ministry recently flagged the possibility of diversion of urea based on e-way bills as it found trucks were taking detours or making multiple stops. A parliamentary panel too had flagged concerns over diversion of urea, especially in border districts.Officials said the alleged diversion of subsidised urea from some of the bordering districts in UP, Rajasthan, Punjab and Bihar has also raised doubts if they are also being smuggled out of the country. The highest 37 districts being assessed for overconsumption of urea are in UP, followed by 16 each in Bihar and Tamil Nadu, and 14 each in Punjab and Gujarat. The 20 districts that were later added for further examinations are in Karnataka, Rajasthan, MP and Maharashtra.India's total urea consumption is estimated at around 400 LMT a year, of which more than 100 LMT are imported. Even for domestic production, it requires a huge amount of imported LPG, as the fuel constitutes 90% of the input cost of urea. Over-consumption of subsidised urea raises additional subsidy burden on the energy bill and increases our import dependence, besides adding to greenhouse gas emissions, an official said."As agricultural urea is universally subsidised, substantial volumes have historically been diverted into non-agricultural sectors. Technical grade urea is a core commercial raw material in resins, glues, plywood fabrication, crockery manufacturing, cattle feed, and commercial explosives," the official added.
Article Summary: CAG has initiated an all-India performance audit of fertiliser subsidy. Audit will look into the alleged diversion of subsidised urea in at least 169 districts across a few states. The audit is likely to be completed by mid-2027 to be tabled by the winter session of Parliament.

NEW DELHI: Centre has made weekly stock declarations mandatory for all pulses by stockists, millers, wholesalers, retailers and large chain retailers, in a move to prevent artificial price rises and curb hoarding. The declarations will have to be uploaded every Friday onto a dedicated portal of the consumer affairs department.The move comes amid a sharp rise in pulse prices despite comfortable supply and record buffer stocks. This comes a week after the food department made weekly stock declarations mandatory for six varieties of rice.Consumer affairs secretary Nidhi Khare said the weekly reporting requirement was aimed at checking sharp price spikes, artificial supply constraints, speculative stock accumulation, hoarding and profiteering. The department has also written to states and UTs, asking them to closely monitor pulse prices and take action against hoarding and black marketing.The department has warned that misreporting of stocks will be viewed seriously and urged traders and millers to rationalise margins and pass on the benefits of favourable supply conditions to consumers.Officials said that the department, in a meeting with millers, has flagged that retail prices of some varieties of pulses were rising despite a decline or minor increase in wholesale prices, robust availability and imports.“So, the increase is likely due to some artificial reasons, including hoarding,” said an official.Govt data show that the average retail prices of tur and gram (chana) stood at Rs 135 and Rs 95 per kg respectively on Friday, registering an increase of 19.5% and 10% from a year ago. Retail inflation in the pulses category rose to 8.7% in Oct, against a deflation of 1.7% in April 2026.Khare said chana production stood at 12.6 million tonne in the 2025-26 crop year, the second highest in five years, while mandi arrivals remained comparable with previous years. Imports of yellow peas, used as a substitute for chana, have also been higher than in previous years. In such a condition, there is no reason for any increase in retail prices.As per official assessment, stocks held by large retailers, dealers, importers, millers, stockists and traders declined from 5.9 million tonne on July 3 to 5.4 million tonne on Nov 6. The Centre’s buffer stock of pulses has touched a record 3.8 million tonne, above the norm of 3.5 million tonne.

NEW DELHI: Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited on Friday said all E20 petrol samples tested across 27 states and Union Territories were found to be within the prescribed ethanol content range of 19-21%.The clarification came amid concerns triggered by a photograph shared during the company's consumer awareness initiative in Karnataka, which showed an ethanol separation test being conducted at one of its fuel stations.In a statement, BPCL said the quality monitoring exercise was carried out by oil marketing companies in coordination with the Centre for High Technology. The company tested 280 samples as part of the exercise.BPCL said its officers had been conducting demonstrations across Karnataka to address consumer queries about E20 petrol and explain the testing procedure.The test involves mixing 100 ml of E20 Ethanol Blended Motor Spirit (EBMS) with 30 ml of water to separate ethanol from petrol."The mixture initially appears hazy or milky, which is normal during the process. It takes time for the ethanol-water and petrol layers to separate completely," the company said.Explaining the photograph that triggered concerns, BPCL said it was inadvertently captured and shared before the separation process was complete, showing an intermediate stage of the test rather than the final reading."The image therefore reflected an intermediate stage of the test and not the final reading," BPCL said.The company added that the officer concerned promptly removed the post after realising that it could be misinterpreted. It maintained that the sample tested was within the prescribed specifications.BPCL said the quality of E20 petrol supplied through its retail outlets was monitored through established quality assurance mechanisms in accordance with Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) specifications under IS 17021.The company urged consumers and other stakeholders to rely on verified testing procedures and prescribed quality assessment mechanisms while evaluating fuel quality.BPCL operates more than 25,300 fuel stations across the country and has a combined refining capacity of approximately 35.3 million metric tonnes per annum across its Mumbai, Kochi and Bina refineries.The company reiterated its commitment to maintaining fuel quality, transparency and consumer confidence.
Article Summary: BPCL said all E20 petrol samples tested across 27 states and Union Territories were found to be within the prescribed ethanol content range of 19-21%. NEW DELHI: The Centre on Friday declared radical Islamic preacher Zakir Naik ’s NGO Islamic Research Foundation , (IRF), as an ‘unlawful association’ for a further period of five years, on the ground that the outfit and its members, particularly Dr Naik, have been encouraging and aiding others to promote disharmony, enmity and ill-will between different religious communities and groups.IRF was first banned under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, on Nov 2016 for five years, and the ban renewed in 2021 for another five years.Announcing the latest extension of the ban until Nov 2031 on his ‘X’ handle, home minister Amit Shah posted: “In steadfast adherence to Modi Ji's vision of zero tolerance towards terrorism and anti-national activities, the MHA hereby extends the ban on the Islamic Research Foundation as an unlawful association under the UAPA.“Led by fugitive terror preacher Dr. Zakir Naik, the organisation has been involved in sinister anti-India designs, including inciting communal hatred, fostering hostility and promoting terrorism. The group has been found to be propagating a venomous ideology of terrorism and separatism, instigating violent unrest, encouraging the regrouping of absconding terrorists and fomenting communal discord”.Naik is said to be based in Malaysia as a permanent resident.Though India has been demanding his extradition, Malaysia has parried the request, purportedly in view of the likely political cost, given the country’s Muslim-majority status and the high following Naik enjoys among the local Muslim community. India had last submitted its extradition request to Malaysia in 2018, followed by a diplomatic note in 2020.Though NIA has been pursuing INTERPOL for issuance of a red-corner notice against Naik since 2017, the multilateral agency has not entertained the request. Naik has thus been travelling in and out of Malaysia, including to the Gulf countries, to deliver his religious sermons. He has not been to India since he left the country in mid-2016. However his name cropped in several terror investigations, including into cases like the 2016 Dhaka Artisan Cafe terror attack and ones relating to ISIS modules recruited in India.MHA said Naik has been making radical statements and speeches to millions of people worldwide through international satellite TV networks, internet, print and social media. The Centre said that unless the unlawful activities of IRF were curbed, it shall continue its subversive activities and re-organise its activists who are still absconding; disrupt the secular fabric of the country by polluting the minds of the people; create communal disharmony; propagate anti-national sentiments; and escalate secessionism by supporting militancy.
Article Summary: The Centre on Friday declared radical Islamic preacher Zakir Naik ’s NGO Islamic Research Foundation as an ‘unlawful association’ for a further period of five years. The outfit and its members have been encouraging and aiding others to promote disharmony, enmity and ill-will between different religious communities and groups. Naik is said to be based in Malaysia as a permanent resident.

When Skål International Mysuru handed its Tourism Excellence Award for wellness to the Indus Valley Ayurvedic Centre at this year's Mysore Travel Mart, it put a stamp on something that has been quietly building for a quarter of a century. Mysuru is no longer only a city of the palace, the yoga schools and the Dasara calendar. It has become a place the world travels to in order to heal, and IVAC is the destination doing most to make that case.The centre has completed more than four lakh treatment journeys and drawn guests from over 65 countries, by its own count, pulling patients from Europe, West Asia and North America to a single campus on the city's edge. Those are the numbers of an institution. And they point to a shift in the map of Indian wellness tourism, where one southern state has long held the story to itself.It is undeniable that in the post-Covid pandemic, Ayurveda and Naturopathy gained immense popularity across the globe with people looking for alternative systems of healthcare and medication. This is exactly what the founder of Indus Valley Ayurvedic Centre Dr Talavane Krishna was striving for, “to bring Ayurveda to the forefront of modern medicine by serving people with ancient wisdom of Ayurveda in modern concepts.”The World Health Organisation (WHO) has recognised the importance of traditional systems of medicines with its theme catalysing ancient wisdom and modern science for the health of people and the planet. Nearly 88 per cent of all countries use traditional medicines, often finding solutions in AyurvedaAyurveda has long drawn interest from travellers; building confidence in its practice and outcomes is a more nuanced undertaking. Foreign guests increasingly want proof before they commit to a residential programme, and a sector built on word of mouth has struggled to give it to them.What distinguishes the place, though, is its language. IVAC talks in clinical terms. Its founder frames the difference as.” In a market thick with cure-all promises, that restraint has become its own kind of marketing.The visitors are the visible half of the story. The quieter half is work. Running residential wellness programmes on this scale demands trained therapists, a skilled job that cannot be sent offshore and that draws its recruits from Mysuru and the districts around it.The centre's associated Foundation trains therapists of its own, and that is where the local stakes sit. As the wellness circuit grows, so does its appetite for young people, who can be taught a craft and moved into steady, skilled employment. A guest's stay is a transaction that ends at checkout. A therapist's career is a livelihood that stays in the city long after.India's Ayurveda-tourism map has carried a single dominant name for decades. IVAC's rise suggests a second one is forming, and not by imitation. Mysuru's advantage is its own: a heritage-and-yoga tourism base that wellness can attach to, a physician-led model that reassures internationalA more visible role from the state could give this momentum further direction. While Karnataka has successfully positioned its technology sector on the global stage, wellness tourism has yet to receive a comparable push through dedicated branding, streamlined medical travel processes or curated circuits connecting established centres. In the meantime, institutions such as IVAC continue to build recognition through their own work and reputation, gradually strengthening Mysuru's identity as a wellness destination.Taken alone, the award on IVAC's wall is a local honour. Set against the guests, the credentials and the numbers behind it, it reads as an early marker of Mysuru's arrival as India's next Ayurveda capital, and of the centre that helped put it there.Visit the website for more details.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday said that ancient Indian astronomers closely studied the cosmos and the movements of planets despite not having access to modern equipment.He also highlighted how India’s space technology is being used to improve people’s lives, from helping fishermen during storms to tracking trains and supporting crop insurance.Addressing a gathering after inaugurating the state-of-the-art COSMOS Planetarium at the University of Mysore campus in Mysuru, PM Modi said India had a rich tradition of scientific study.“India has produced many great astronomers, including Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Bhaskaracharya and Nilakantha Somayaji,” he said.“Despite not having access to the advanced technology and instruments available today, they made remarkable discoveries and performed some of the most complex calculations. Today, as India continues to achieve one milestone after another in the field of science, Mysuru, through the state-of-the-art COSMOS Planetarium, is adding a new chapter to India's scientific journey,” he said.He recalled how ancient Indian astronomers studied the cosmos and calculated the movements of stars and planets despite not having access to modern technology.“Our ancestors studied the sky very closely. They understood the movements of stars and planets, and they created calendars. They calculated solar and lunar eclipses,” he added.The Prime Minister said India’s space programme was not limited to achievements beyond Earth but also contributed to the welfare of people through practical applications. Isro has developed a satellite communication system for our fishermen; boats equipped with receivers can receive timely alerts during storms, and their safe return to the shore can be monitored. Many of you likely check the live location of trains to see where they are and when they will arrive at a station—this is made possible by a real-time train tracking system developed by the Indian Railways and Isro," he said."Similarly, satellite data is utilised in the 'Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana' where information from fields combined with satellite data is used to estimate crop yields, estimates that form the basis for determining farmers' insurance claims. In short, while our satellites are reaching great heights in space, they are simultaneously being used to improve the lives of people here on Earth," he added.Drawing a parallel between the planetarium and the Viveka Smaraka, which he had inaugurated earlier, PM Modi said the two institutions reflected India's spiritual and scientific traditions.“The Viveka Smaraka inspires us to look within and seek spiritual wisdom, while a visit to the Cosmos Planetarium draws our gaze toward the sky, motivating us to explore this vast universe and unravel its mysteries. This serves as an example of how, in India, the traditions of spirituality and science have always progressed hand in hand,” he said.The Prime Minister said the government's decision to open up the space sector had created new opportunities for private companies and startups. He also cited India's achievements in satellite docking and undocking and sending an Indian astronaut to the International Space Station (ISS).“For a long time, our country has embraced the call of ‘Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan’. Atal Ji added ‘Jai Vigyan’ to it, and I further added ‘Jai Anusandhan’. India in the 21st century is moving forward with this very vision, and our youth are performing exceptionally well in this endeavour,” he said.“Last year, India hosted the International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics in Mumbai. Our young participants took part in it with great enthusiasm,” he added.Earlier in the day, PM also inaugurated the Pink Line of Bengaluru’s Namma Metro, highlighting the expansion of the city’s public transport network and its role in improving connectivity.Addressing the inauguration ceremony, he said Bengaluru had become the third city in the country, after Delhi-NCR and the Mumbai Metropolitan Region, to have a metro network spanning 100 km."After Delhi-NCR and the Mumbai Metropolitan Region, Bengaluru is the third city in the country where the metro network has reached 100 km," he said."With this new metro line, connectivity between Bengaluru and numerous educational institutions will be further improved. Furthermore, areas known as major business, technology, and commercial centres in Bengaluru will also be connected by the metro," he added.The Prime Minister said the metro expansion reflected the government's focus on improving ease of living and travel, and would help commuters save time and money.The planetarium inaugurated by PM Modi is located on the University of Mysore campus at the foothills of Chamundi Hills. It is India's first LED dome planetarium.PM Modi also praised the Mysuru royal family for its contribution to promoting science and education, including the establishment of the University of Mysore and the donation of land for the Indian Institute of Science (IISc).
Article Summary: PM Modi said ancient Indian astronomers studied the cosmos and the movements of planets despite not having access to modern equipment. He highlighted how India's space technology is being used to improve people’s lives, from helping fishermen during storms to tracking trains and supporting crop insurance.

Article Title: 'Why silent on Haryana?' Punjab CM Mann hits out at BJP-led Centre over stubble-burning
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann on Friday questioned the Centre's response to stubble burning in neighbouring Haryana , accusing the BJP-led government of singling out Punjab over Delhi's air pollution. He alleged that the state was being blamed even before the paddy harvesting season had begun.Addressing a press conference, Mann argued that the movement of winds did not support claims that smoke from Punjab was directly responsible for Delhi's deteriorating air quality. He said smoke would take at least three days to reach the national capital even if winds blew from the north-west at a speed of 100 kmph."We have been saying that Punjab smoke will reach Delhi if the wind blows north to west with a speed of at least 100 kmph, and then also, it will take three days to reach. But the wind does not blow from north to west; it blows from east to west or west to east. Why don't they tell anything to Haryana?" news agency PTI quoted him as saying.Pointing out that Haryana and Uttar Pradesh also cultivate paddy, Mann questioned why these states were not held equally responsible for pollution in Delhi. He also took a dig at reports that authorities in Pakistan's Punjab had linked stubble burning in Indian Punjab to poor air quality in Lahore."So, does the smoke from here reach there as well?" he asked.The chief minister also brought up the issue of paddy procurement, contrasting Punjab's performance with that of Haryana. He said the state had already met its procurement target of 180 lakh metric tonnes and was expected to purchase around 200 lakh metric tonnes."Paddy is grown there also. They keep giving us lessons to learn from Haryana on MSP, but what is the state of paddy procurement there whereas in Punjab we have met the procurement target. Rather, we will far exceed it by procuring 200 lakh metric tonnes against 180 lakh metric tonnes. We will procure every single grain of farmers," Mann said.He alleged that Punjab was being unfairly targeted by BJP leaders, specifically referring to Delhi minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa, who he claimed had blamed the state even before harvesting started.Mann said stubble management required a coordinated approach involving all affected states rather than placing the responsibility solely on Punjab. He called on the Centre to bring together states across north India to work out a long-term solution."Now, you will take 200 lakh metric tonne from us, there will be stubble. So, why does the Centre not find a solution?" he said."The prime minister finds a solution to global problems; this issue is a problem of the entire North India. So, they should make these three to four states sit and find a solution," he added.
Article Summary: Bhagwant Mann questions why Haryana is not held accountable for stubble burning. He accuses Centre of targeting Punjab over Delhi's air pollution. Mann argues that the movement of winds did not support claims that smoke from Punjab was directly responsible for Delhi's deteriorating air quality.

Article Title: Pakistani beauty cream seized in Maharashtra found with mercury 48,000 times over limit
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Beauty creams worth nearly Rs 40 lakh seized from a shop in Maharashtra's Nanded have been found to contain dangerously high concentrations of mercury, with one product recording levels more than 48,000 times the permissible limit, according to a government laboratory report.The findings come months after the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) flagged Pakistani-origin skin-lightening creams for excessive levels of toxic metals and ordered an immediate halt to the sale and distribution of three products. In September, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) also issued a public health alert against two Pakistani-labelled whitening creams, warning that they were unauthorised for sale in India and contained heavy metals beyond specified limits.The latest laboratory findings relate to products seized by Nanded police during a raid at Afrah Collection, also known as Afrah Tours and Travels, in the Makkah Galli area on July 9. The seized stock was valued at around Rs 39.69 lakh.Tests of samples collected during the raid found that PARLEY 24K Gold Gleam Beauty Cream contained 48,453.44 parts per million (PPM) of mercury, against the permissible limit of 1 PPM.GOREE Beauty Cream with Lycopene was found to contain 6,924.94 PPM of mercury.The raid was carried out by a team from Itwara police station along with Food and Drug Administration officials. Police identified the shop operator as Mohammad Ziauddin Mohammad Wajid, who was found stocking cosmetics carrying labels in Urdu and English claiming Pakistani origin.The development follows a Maharashtra FDA alert issued in July against three skin-lightening products, including Goree Beauty Cream, which was identified as being of Pakistani origin. The regulator had ordered an immediate stop to their use, sale and distribution after laboratory tests detected excessive mercury and lead. The other products named were Face Fresh Gold Beauty Cream and Serum, and Golden Star Beauty Cream. The FDA also flagged missing mandatory labelling information, including manufacturer details and batch and expiry dates.In September, CDSCO separately named Goree Beauty Cream and Chandni Whitening Cream in a public health alert dated September 8. It said neither had received the required registration certificate for import and sale in India and advised consumers not to buy or use them. Sellers and distributors were also directed to stop their sale and promotion.Officials have warned that prolonged exposure to excessive mercury and other toxic heavy metals through cosmetics can cause serious health problems, including skin disorders, kidney damage and neurological complications.A case has been registered in Nanded under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act. Police have urged people to report the sale of counterfeit, unlicensed or suspicious imported products.
Article Summary: One product recorded levels more than 48,000 times the permissible limit. The findings come months after the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration flagged Pakistani-origin skin-lightening creams for excessive levels of toxic metals. The products were seized during a raid at Afrah Collection, also known as Afrah Tours and Travels, in the Makkah Galli area.

Article Title: 'Potential to disturb public peace': Centre refuses RTI on 'Any Kuki Tribes' deletion proposal
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: The Centre has refused to disclose details of a reported Manipur government proposal to delete the nomenclature "Any Kuki Tribes" from the state's Scheduled Tribes (ST) list, citing concerns that sharing the information could aggravate inter-community tensions in the violence-hit state, PTI reported.The Central Information Commission (CIC), while hearing an RTI appeal, upheld the ministry of tribal affairs' decision to withhold the information, saying the public interest in disclosing internal deliberations did not outweigh the potential risks to public order.The RTI application was filed by an applicant Micheal Haokip, who referred to a Manipur government letter that he claimed concerned a proposal to remove "Any Kuki Tribes" from the state's ST list and replace "Any Mizo (Lushai) Tribe" with "Mizo".Haokip had sought confirmation of whether the ministry received the proposal, along with its date of receipt and official file number. He also sought details of the action taken, whether it had been forwarded to the Registrar General of India (RGI) and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) for concurrence, and copies of relevant communications and file notings.In its reply dated June 24, 2025, the ministry said it was the nodal authority for processing claims relating to the inclusion, exclusion or modification of communities in the ST list under Article 342 of the Constitution.It said proposals recommended and justified by the concerned state government or Union Territory administration could be processed further, subject to concurrence from the RGI and NCST, before being considered for legislative amendment.The ministry argued that disclosing information during the examination and consultation process could exert "undue pressure and influence" on authorities and allow vested interests to interfere with independent decision-making.It also cited instances where disclosure of information relating to the notification of a community had allegedly led to violence."Such disclosure of information will have the potential to disturb public peace, tranquillity and encourage enmity between the communities," the CPIO said.During the CIC hearing, the ministry reiterated that the matter was sensitive given the ethnic violence and prevailing law-and-order concerns in Manipur. It apprehended that premature disclosure of internal proposals, communications and deliberative records could aggravate inter-community tensions, exert pressure on authorities and potentially disturb public order.Haokip argued that the ministry's response was vague and failed to explain how basic administrative details, such as the date of receipt, file number and names of officials handling the matter, could be treated as information held in a fiduciary capacity.He also contended that the public-order concerns cited by the ministry were general and speculative.The CIC, however, said it was not persuaded that the public interest in disclosing substantive internal deliberations and communications outweighed the potential harm identified by the ministry.It also examined whether non-sensitive portions of the records could be disclosed after redaction under Section 10 of the RTI Act but rejected even the limited relief of providing redacted copies of the proposal and related action-taken notings.
Article Summary: The Centre has refused to disclose details of a reported Manipur government proposal to delete the nomenclature "Any Kuki Tribes" from the state's Scheduled Tribes (ST) list. The Central Information Commission (CIC) upheld the ministry of tribal affairs' decision to withhold the information.

NEW DELHI: Congress on Friday stepped up its attack on the Centre over two-year high retail inflation, describing the current economic situation as "mehengaai ka bhuchaal" (earthquake of inflation) rather than "Amrit Kaal". The opposition party alleged that households were struggling to manage their budgets as food prices and the cost of everyday necessities continued to climb."Under the Modi government, inflation is no longer just a witch—it has now become an uninvited guest, devouring every household’s budget. From the kitchen to every other daily necessity, prices have spiraled out of control. The Modi government’s misguided policies have broken the backs of ordinary people," Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said in a post on X.Referring to the latest inflation figures, he said that retail inflation had climbed to 6.09 per cent, its highest level in two years, while prices had increased across 11 of the 12 consumption categories. He also questioned the government's response to the rising cost of living.Ramesh flagged food inflation at 8.94 per cent and pointed to sharp increases in the prices of essential vegetables and other household items.Citing figures, he said onions had become 116 per cent more expensive, garlic 60 per cent and ginger 48 per cent. He added that prices of flour, cooking oil, ghee, milk, pulses and soap had also been rising."Inflation has been rising for the past 12 years, and its real impact is far greater than government statistics suggest. But this year, even those figures have been rising every month. Retail inflation has reached a two-year high of 6.09%. What is surprising is that inflation has risen in 11 of the 12 consumption categories, yet the arrogant minister of propaganda has remained silent about his government’s performance," he said.The Congress leader further raised concerns over companies potentially reducing product quantities even as prices increase. He also warned that any increase in interest rates could add to the financial burden on households by making loans and everyday expenses costlier."Food inflation has reached 8.94%. Onions have become 116% more expensive, garlic 60%, and ginger 48%. Inflation is running rampant across everything, from flour, oil, ghee, milk and lentils to soap. Besides raising prices, companies are considering reducing product quantities. Now there are also fears of interest rate hikes, which would make both borrowing and living even more expensive for ordinary people.This is not an Amrit Kaal; it is an inflationary earthquake," he said.The Congress had also criticised the Centre on Thursday over the rising cost of essential commodities, alleging that mounting household expenses were putting pressure on ordinary consumers and calling for effective steps to rein in inflation.

NEW DELHI: The commission set up to investigate the ethnic violence that broke out in Manipur in May 2023 received its seventh extension on Friday, with the Centre directing it to submit its report by May 20, 2027, according to a government order.The commission was initially given a deadline of November 2023 to submit its findings under a notification issued in September that year.Its terms of reference included investigating the causes and spread of the violence that broke out in Manipur on May 3, 2023, targeting members of different communities, and examining the sequence of events that led to the unrest.It was also asked to assess whether there had been any lapses or negligence on the part of officials or other individuals, and whether the administrative steps taken to prevent and contain the violence were adequate.The ethnic clashes have claimed more than 300 lives and forced thousands to flee their homes, widening the divide between the Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities.With the latest extension, the commission will have nearly four years to complete an inquiry that was originally expected to conclude within a few months.

Article Title: Watch: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay launches one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns
Article Text:
Vijay presented 22-carat, one-gram gold rings to 25 newborns. (PTI)

Who is eligible for the gold ring?

Scheme draws on Tamil tradition

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. He also held some of the newborns and presented the rings to beneficiaries during the launch programme.Under the scheme, eligible babies born in government hospitals and government primary health centres will receive a 22-carat, one-gram gold ring.The initiative, named the Maternal Uncle Gold Ring Scheme (Thaaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam), has an annual allocation of Rs 755.83 crore.It is aimed at celebrating motherhood, promoting maternal and child health and encouraging institutional deliveries by increasing public confidence in government healthcare facilities.The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions.Mothers must be registered under the Pregnancy and Infant Cohort Monitoring and Evaluation (PICME) system and have a Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) ID. They will also have to provide an e-KYC-verified Aadhaar card along with one of the prescribed identity or residence documents.These include ration cards, voter identity cards, Labour Welfare Board identity cards, Department of Posts address cards and nativity certificates.The state government has already procured 1.28 lakh one-gram gold rings for the initial rollout. Each ring will have a unique serial number and will be packed in tamper-proof packaging.From Monday, babies born in government hospitals will receive the rings at the time of discharge, according to the state government.To clear the backlog of eligible babies born between June 22 and Monday, the government will distribute the rings through 107 hubs across Tamil Nadu.Distribution will begin at the rate of 100 babies per day at each hub. At designated centres, 25 beneficiaries will be accommodated in the morning and another 25 in the afternoon to avoid overcrowding, PTI reported.Village Health Nurses will distribute invitations informing beneficiaries of their allotted date and time. Beneficiaries have been asked to visit the designated centres only at the time mentioned in their invitations.The district administration has also made transportation arrangements for beneficiaries from their respective areas. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election as a symbolic gift to newborns, drawing on the Tamil tradition of ‘Thaimaaman Seer’. The scheme has retrospective effect from June 22, Vijay’s birthday.A government order issued on June 23 described the initiative as a token celebrating the birth of a child, motherhood and the cultural tradition of ‘Thaimaaman’.According to ANI, Tamil Nadu minister Arun Raj explained the cultural significance of the initiative saying, "A maternal uncle is someone who is among the first to rush in when a child is born, sharing in his sister’s happiness as his own. He assures her that he will always stand by her and her child, offering love, support and a sense of security.""Today, the Tamil Nadu Government, under the leadership of our brother, Mr. Vijay, is embracing this sacred bond of the maternal uncle and, as a gesture of that affection, is set to provide a one-gram gold ring to every child born in government hospitals. When the scheme was announced and the question arose as to where it should be launched, the place chosen by our Chief Minister was Madurai. This is the sacred soil of Madurai, blessed with the compassion and grace of Mother Meenakshi," he added.Tamil Nadu records around 7.8 lakh deliveries annually, with institutional deliveries accounting for 99.9% of births, according to NFHS-6. Government health facilities account for nearly 4.2 lakh deliveries, or around 53% of the total.According to the state government, the average out-of-pocket expenditure for a delivery at a government hospital is Rs 1,364, compared with Rs 63,473 at a private hospital.The government said the scheme is intended to encourage safe institutional deliveries, strengthen maternal and child welfare and increase public trust in government healthcare services.The Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation will procure the gold rings based on annual requirements, while a project and programme management unit will oversee implementation and monitoring.
Article Summary: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election.

NEW DELHI: Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday said the garbage mountains at the city's landfill sites were steadily shrinking as she reviewed waste disposal work at Okhla and laid the foundation stone for new waste processing facilities at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola.Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years, with a large portion of the cleared area also being turned green.She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed."Today, at Okhla, we have processed almost all the legacy waste that was there before January 2025," Gupta said.Gupta said the government was working on two fronts: clearing the existing garbage mountains while ensuring that fresh waste generated every day did not accumulate into new landfill sites.According to news agency ANI, she said around 3,000-4,000 metric tonnes of fresh waste reaches the sites daily and is being processed round the clock."The garbage currently piled up here is essentially fresh waste generated after January 2025, and that too is being processed round the clock. So, we are fighting on two fronts: one is eliminating waste, and the other is ensuring that the 3,000 to 4,000 metric tons of fresh waste arriving daily is processed immediately, so that new garbage mountains are not formed for future generations," Gupta said.She said the government was working to reduce the existing garbage mountains to zero."People are seeing that the garbage mountains are continuously shrinking and soon a time will come when they will become zero," Gupta said.Gupta also said she had taken what she described as her "last selfie" with the garbage mountain at Okhla."Today I have taken my last selfie with the garbage mountain; after this I have taken a pledge that this garbage mountain will end soon," she said.Taking a jibe at the Opposition, Gupta added, "I had said - garbage mountain, you will have to go; the opposition mocked. Today I will say the garbage mountain is going; now only its back remains."During the programme at the Okhla SLF site, Gupta laid the foundation stone for fresh waste processing plants at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola, as well as a biogas facility at Ghazipur. She also inaugurated the M&CW Centre at Kotla Mubarakpur through virtual mode from Okhla.The Okhla plant will be built at a cost of Rs 103 crore and will have a processing capacity of 1,400 metric tonnes per day.The Singhola facility will cost Rs 42 crore and have a capacity of 800 metric tonnes per day, while the Ghazipur plant will have a processing capacity of 700 metric tonnes per day.The facilities are intended to process fresh waste as well as construction and demolition waste. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure."Waste should not remain waste; Delhi should use it as wealth," she said, adding that new technologies were being introduced for waste segregation and processing.She said waste and cattle dung would be used to produce biogas and manure as part of efforts to build a technology-driven waste management system.Gupta said the government was taking up several measures to address pollution, including work on landfill waste, cleaning the Yamuna, dust mitigation, plantation, road infrastructure and waste management."Our government is tackling pollution from a 360-degree perspective to ensure it gradually decreases. We are working on every aspect, be it addressing the mountains of garbage, cleaning the Yamuna, improving road infrastructure, or managing waste, to ensure the people of Delhi enjoy better air quality. Our resolve and policies are absolutely clear, and we are working 24x7 in the public interest," she said.The chief minister also reviewed the progress of waste disposal work with officials and directed them to accelerate the work according to the stipulated timeline.She said the garbage mountains at Bhalswa, Ghazipur and Okhla had caused inconvenience to people travelling through these areas and said the government was continuing efforts to eliminate them.
Article Summary: Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years.
